track: samidha-navagraha — the nine homa woods of the navagraha (Sanskrit name, botanical identification, locus)
compiledBy: COMPILER agent — cites only snippet ids present in the fetcher ledger persisted at ledgerSources; introduced no source of its own.
whatThisIs: This is a dossier of SAMIDHA — the fuel-sticks fed to the fire in the navagraha homa (grahayajña / grahaśānti) — as four Sanskrit witnesses give them: Yājñavalkyasmṛti 1.302 (yajn-s1), Matsyapurāṇa 93.27 (mats-s1), Agnipurāṇa 164.8 and again 167.6cd–7ab (agni-s1, agni-s3), and Garuḍapurāṇa 1.101.9 (garu-s1). A fifth witness, Atharvavedapariśiṣṭa 26.5.6–5.7 (avp-s1, avp-s2), gives a DIFFERENT nine-item sequence for the same purpose, and it is carried here in full rather than harmonised away. IT IS NOT A LIST OF NAKṢATRA TREES (nakṣatra-vanaspati) AND IT IS NOT A LIST OF INCENSE (dhūpa). Those are different things with different textual homes, and merging all three into one 'Vedic plants' column is the error this dossier exists to refuse. The distinction is visible inside a single witness: Yājñavalkya prescribes nine different samidhs graha by graha (yajn-s1) but a single undifferentiated incense — guggulu — for the whole rite (yajn-s4, Yj 1.299a). Nine woods, one incense, in the same passage. A third conflation is live in the current literature and is flagged rather than used: the navagraha vāṭikā, a nine-planet GARDEN with a planting direction for each graha (ijcrt-s1, ijcrt-s4), which is about what is planted and where, not about what is burned. This dossier records what the texts say is offered. It records no efficacy, no quantity, no process parameter, and no outcome.
scopeNote: A samidh is fuel. The Matsyapurāṇa frames the passage as homa in the verse immediately before the list (mats-s2, MatsP 93.26) and adds that each samidh is offered separately with its own mantra (mats-s3, MatsP 93.30); Yājñavalkya opens the section as a grahayajña undertaken by one who desires prosperity or śānti (yajn-s3, Yj 1.295); the Atharvavedapariśiṣṭa chapter is titled samillakṣaṇam, 'the characteristics of samidhs' (avp-s3), and closes its planetary passage as a response to graha and nakṣatra affliction (avp-s4). The dossier carries the assignment and the locus. It carries no counts, no measures, no timings and no procedure.

entries.forWhat: Sūrya (the Sun) — position 1 in the mainstream sequence
entries.toxicFlag: The latex is hazardous on contact. Basak et al. 2009 report that Calotropis latex contains alkaloids described as caustic and considered poisonous (basak-s1), and that every affected eye in their series showed mild to severe corneal oedema with Descemet's folds (basak-s2). SPECIES MISMATCH, STATED: that study is of Calotropis procera; Monier-Williams identifies arka as C. gigantea (mw-arka); the ledger's own note records that both are called arka/madār and does not equate them. No source in this ledger reports on the smoke or on combustion, so nothing here speaks to burning.
entries.variants: Vernacular Hindi आक āk in a nine-name list (pp-s1) and ऑक in the same page's eight-graha list (pp-s2), both Tier C. 'madaara' in the Kanchi Kamakoti paraphrase of the Matsya Purāṇa (kkm-s1, Tier C). English 'Arka' in both public-domain translations (vidya-s1; gdutt-s1). CONFLATION FLAG, not a variant: the navagraha-vāṭikā literature also gives Sūrya Calotropis gigantea (L.) Dryand, Asclepiadaceae — but as a plant to be PLANTED at the centre of a garden, with no locus cited for the assignment (ijcrt-s2, ijcrt-s5, Tier C).
entries.note: Attested at Yj 1.302 (yajn-s1), MatsP 93.27 (mats-s1), AP 164.8 (agni-s1), AP 167.6cd (agni-s3) and GarP 1.101.9 (garu-s1). The graha order that 'kramāt' ('in order') refers back to is fixed by Yj 1.296 (yajn-s2) and AP 164.2 (agni-s4), both of which run Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, Ketu; the Mitākṣarā gloss on v. 302 states the same, 'for the nine planets beginning with Sūrya in their respective order' (vidya-s3). Vidyarnava's 1918 public-domain translation renders the pairing explicitly (vidya-s1), under a printed heading 'The Samidh fuel' and a translator's rubric naming the subject as the woods the fire-sticks are made from (vidya-s4).

entries.forWhat: Candra / Soma (the Moon) — position 2 in the mainstream sequence
entries.botanical: Butea frondosa (Monier-Williams 1899, s.v. palāśa, printed in the abbreviated form 'B° F°') / Butea monosperma (Boddupalli & Sastri 2015, Tier B, on the sruk). BOTH ARE CARRIED: no source in this ledger states that the two names denote the same taxon.
entries.variants: Vernacular ढाक ḍhāk (pp-s1, Tier C); 'palaasha' (kkm-s1); 'Palasa' (vidya-s1), 'Palasha' (gdutt-s1). TIER C LOSS: the same Tier C page that lists ढाक among nine samidhs (pp-s1) omits the Moon entirely from its per-graha table, which is headed 'nine plants of the navagraha' and names only eight grahas (pp-s2).
entries.note: Attested at Yj 1.302 (yajn-s1), MatsP 93.27 (mats-s1, in the dual compound palāśakhadirau), AP 164.8 (agni-s1, spelt pālāśa), AP 167.6cd (agni-s3) and GarP 1.101.9 (garu-s1). Palāśa is not graha-specific in the wider corpus: it heads the five-wood samidh list of Bṛhatsaṃhitā 43.12 in the army-lustration rite (bs-s1) and appears in the Śāṅkhāyanagṛhyasūtra 4.17.3 nine-plant handful (sgs-s1), neither of which has any planetary assignment (bs-s2, sgs-s2).

entries.forWhat: Maṅgala / Mahīputra (Mars) — position 3 in the mainstream sequence
entries.botanical: Mimosa catechu (Monier-Williams 1899, s.v. khadira) / Acacia catechu (Boddupalli & Sastri 2015, Tier B) / Senegalia catechu (L.f.) P.J.H. Hurter & Mabb., Fabaceae (IJCRT 2026, Tier C, in a garden context). ALL THREE ARE CARRIED. All three carry the specific epithet catechu — that is an observation about the strings, and no source in this ledger states that the three names denote the same taxon.
entries.variants: Vernacular कत्था kattha in the nine-name list (pp-s1) and खैर khair in the per-graha list on the same Tier C page (pp-s2); 'khaira' (kkm-s1). MANUSCRIPT VARIANT AT THIS POSITION: Mitra's footnote to Agnipurāṇa 164.8 records that mss ga, gha and ña read 'khadiras tv apāmārgo 'tha' where his text prints 'khadiro hy apāmārgotha' (agni-s2); the Garuḍapurāṇa e-text prints that same reading, 'khadirastvapāmārgo 'tha' (garu-s1). The variant is a sandhi/particle difference and does not change which plant sits at which position — that is the compiler's reading of the two e-texts side by side, not a published collation.
entries.note: Attested at Yj 1.302 (yajn-s1), MatsP 93.27 (mats-s1), AP 164.8 (agni-s1), AP 167.6cd (agni-s3) and GarP 1.101.9 (garu-s1). Khadira is not graha-specific in the wider corpus: it heads the Bṛhatsaṃhitā 43.12 nīrājana samidh list (bs-s1), opens the tooth-stick effect list at BS 84.5 (bs-s3), and — cited by locus only, with no text reproduced under FRAMING §5 C-5 — carries a non-planetary vaśīkaraṇa use at Atharvavedapariśiṣṭa 36.7.1 (avp-s5).

entries.forWhat: Budha / Somaputra (Mercury) — position 4 in the mainstream sequence
entries.botanical: Achyranthes aspera (Monier-Williams 1899, s.v. apāmārga — one of the three headwords retrieved byte-exact from Cologne)
entries.variants: Vernacular चिरचिटा circiṭā (pp-s1) and लटजीरा laṭjīrā (pp-s2), both Tier C; 'chichinda' in the Kanchi Kamakoti paraphrase, where the ledger's own note identifies it as standing for apāmārga (kkm-s1).
entries.note: Attested at Yj 1.302 (yajn-s1), MatsP 93.27 (mats-s1), AP 164.8 (agni-s1), AP 167.6cd (agni-s3) and GarP 1.101.9 (garu-s1). MW records apāmārga as 'employed very often in incantations, in medicine, in washing linen, and in sacrifices' and cites it to the Atharvaveda and Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (mw-apamarga) — i.e. its ritual use is attested in the older layer, without any planetary assignment. The gṛhyasūtra sweep confirms that: the sole apāmārga occurrence in the Āśvalāyanagṛhyasūtra is at 2.7.6 in a non-planetary context (gs-sweep-s2), and apāmārga also stands in the Śāṅkhāyana Āgrahāyaṇī handful at 4.17.3 (sgs-s1, sgs-s2).

entries.forWhat: Bṛhaspati (Jupiter) — position 5 in the mainstream sequence
entries.english: 'Peepal' — the word chosen by Vidyarnava's 1918 public-domain translation (vidya-s1)
entries.variants: Vernacular पीपल pīpal in both Tier C lists (pp-s1, pp-s2); 'peepul' (kkm-s1); 'Pippala' (gdutt-s1). Also 'Peepul' in a GENERAL, non-graha-assigned homa list (kst-s1).
entries.note: NO BINOMIAL SHIPS FOR THIS ROW, and the reason is a fetch failure, not an absence in the tradition. Every Tier A witness here reads pippala at this position — yajn-s1, mats-s1, agni-s1, agni-s3, garu-s1 — not aśvattha, which is the word the sequence is usually printed with today. This ledger contains no lexicon entry for the headword pippala: the Cologne Monier-Williams fetch for it returned HTTP 429 then 403, and it was not obtained from the wisdomlib mirror either. Ficus religiosa appears in this ledger only under the DIFFERENT headword aśvattha (mw-asvattha; also bod-s5), and nothing in the ledger equates pippala with aśvattha. Supplying that equation would be an identification no cited source makes, so the botanical field is left empty rather than filled from a parallel.

entries.forWhat: Śukra (Venus) — position 6 in the mainstream sequence
entries.botanical: Ficus glomerata (Monier-Williams 1899, s.v. udumbara — retrieved byte-exact from Cologne) / Ficus racemosa (Boddupalli & Sastri 2015, Tier B, s.v. audumbara). BOTH ARE CARRIED: no source in this ledger states that the two names denote the same taxon.
entries.variants: The witnesses split on the vṛddhi: plain udumbara at Yj 1.302 (yajn-s1) and AP 164.8 / 167.7 (agni-s1, agni-s3); audumbara at MatsP 93.27 (mats-s1) and GarP 1.101.9 (garu-s1). Vernacular गूलर gūlar (pp-s1, pp-s2); 'gular' (kkm-s1, and also in the general non-graha list kst-s1); 'Audumvara' in Dutt's 1908 translation (gdutt-s1).
entries.note: Udumbara is not graha-specific in the wider corpus: it stands in the Bṛhatsaṃhitā 43.12 nīrājana five (bs-s1), in the Śāṅkhāyana Āgrahāyaṇī handful (sgs-s1), and — cited by locus only, text not reproduced under FRAMING §5 C-5 — in a non-planetary vaśīkaraṇa rite at Atharvavedapariśiṣṭa 36.7.1 (avp-s5). Boddupalli & Sastri group audumbara with nyagrodha, aśvattha and plakṣa as the 'naiyagrōdha samidhas' of Taittirīya Saṃhitā 3-4-8.4 (bod-s1), a chapter they describe as naming samidha trees with no planetary assignment (bod-s3).

entries.forWhat: Śanaiścara (Saturn) — position 7 in the mainstream sequence
entries.botanical: Prosopis spicigera, or 'according to others' Mimosa suma — Monier-Williams 1899 prints both readings in the same entry and does not choose (mw-sami).
entries.variants: Vernacular जांड jāṇḍ in the nine-name list (pp-s1) and शमी in the per-graha list (pp-s2), both Tier C. TIER C LOSS: the Kanchi Kamakoti paraphrase of the Matsya Purāṇa navagraha-yajña names only eight woods and śamī is the one missing (kkm-s1) — although MatsP 93.27, the verse it paraphrases, has it (mats-s1). ORDERING DEFECT, separately: pp-s2 lists Śani before Śukra, inverting the order of Yj 1.296 and AP 164.2 (yajn-s2, agni-s4), while still pairing Śani with śamī and Śukra with gūlar/udumbara.
entries.note: Attested at Yj 1.302 (yajn-s1), MatsP 93.27 (mats-s1), AP 164.8 (agni-s1), AP 167.7 (agni-s3) and GarP 1.101.9 (garu-s1); Vidyarnava 1918 renders it 'S^ami', an OCR artefact for śamī (vidya-s2). MW's entry records a fire association independent of any planetary scheme — a very tough hard wood 'supposed to contain fire', and the entry continues on kindling the sacred fire and the Purūravas legend (mw-sami). Śamī also opens the Śāṅkhāyana Āgrahāyaṇī nine-plant handful (sgs-s1), which is not a graha rite (sgs-s2).

entries.forWhat: Rāhu — position 8 in the mainstream sequence
entries.english: 'bent grass, panic grass, Dūrb grass' (Monier-Williams 1899, s.v. dūrvā — retrieved byte-exact from Cologne)
entries.variants: Vernacular दूब dūb (pp-s1) and दूर्वा (pp-s2); 'duub' (kkm-s1); 'Durva' (vidya-s2, gdutt-s1, kst-s1).
entries.note: Attested at Yj 1.302 (yajn-s1), MatsP 93.27 (mats-s1), AP 164.8 (agni-s1, spelt durvā), AP 167.7 (agni-s3) and GarP 1.101.9 (garu-s1). MW glosses dūrvā as a grass and cites it to the Ṛgveda, Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, Brāhmaṇas and Mahābhārata (mw-durva) — so the common English label 'the nine sacred WOODS' is inexact at positions 8 and 9, where the witnesses name grasses. Dutt's 1908 translation registers the same thing by calling the last items 'blades' rather than twigs (gdutt-s1).

entries.forWhat: Ketu — position 9 in the mainstream sequence
entries.english: 'the sacred grass used at certain religious ceremonies'; MW's same entry adds that 'the Brāhmaṇas commonly call it darbha' (mw-kusa)
entries.variants: Vernacular कुशा kuśā in both Tier C lists (pp-s1, pp-s2); 'Kusha' (kkm-s1, gdutt-s1); 'Kusa' (vidya-s2). DIVERGENT MODERN IDENTIFICATION, and it is a garden not a fire: the navagraha-vāṭikā literature assigns Ketu Imperata cylindrica (L.) P.Beauv., Poaceae, naming it 'Darbha or Thatch Grass' and directing that it be PLANTED in the north-west (ijcrt-s3, ijcrt-s4, Tier C). That is a different taxon from MW's Poa cynosuroides, and the source cites no Sanskrit locus for any of its assignments (ijcrt-s5).
entries.note: Attested at Yj 1.302 (yajn-s1), MatsP 93.27 (mats-s1), AP 164.8 (agni-s1), AP 167.7 (agni-s3) and GarP 1.101.9 (garu-s1). Like dūrvā at position 8, kuśa is a grass, not a wood. Kuśa also stands in the Śāṅkhāyana Āgrahāyaṇī handful (sgs-s1), which carries no planetary assignment (sgs-s2).

entries.forWhat: Āditya (the Sun) — position 1 in the DIVERGENT Atharvavedapariśiṣṭa sequence; the only graha this witness names
entries.toxicFlag: Same contact hazard as the mainstream arka row: Calotropis latex is described as caustic and considered poisonous (basak-s1), with corneal oedema in every affected eye of the reported series (basak-s2). The study species is C. procera, not MW's C. gigantea.
entries.note: Atharvavedapariśiṣṭa 26.5.6cd (avp-s1), inside the chapter titled samillakṣaṇam (avp-s3), with the ordering rule at 26.5.7 — 'in order, for the grahas beginning with Āditya' (avp-s2) — and the purpose stated at 26.5.9 as a response to graha and nakṣatra affliction (avp-s4). Position 1 is the only position this witness ties to a named graha, because 'ādityādi' fixes the head of the sequence and nothing else. The mainstream witnesses agree with it here: arka for the Sun (yajn-s1, mats-s1, agni-s1, garu-s1).

entries.forWhat: position 2 in the Atharvavedapariśiṣṭa 26.5.6–5.7 sequence — the graha is not enumerated in this witness
entries.botanical: Butea frondosa (MW 1899, mw-palasa) / Butea monosperma (Boddupalli & Sastri 2015, bod-s6). Both carried; no source here equates them.
entries.note: Atharvavedapariśiṣṭa 26.5.6cd (avp-s1). NO PER-GRAHA ASSIGNMENT IS MADE FOR THIS ROW. The text says only 'in order, for the grahas beginning with Āditya' (avp-s2), and this ledger contains no Atharvavedapariśiṣṭa verse enumerating the nine grahas. Aligning position 2 with the Moon would mean importing the graha order from Yj 1.296 or AP 164.2 (yajn-s2, agni-s4) — a different text — and that is completion from a parallel, which this dossier does not do. It is recorded that the mainstream witnesses also have palāśa at position 2 (yajn-s1, mats-s1, agni-s1, garu-s1), which is a fact about the two sequences and not an assignment.

entries.forWhat: position 3 in the Atharvavedapariśiṣṭa 26.5.6–5.7 sequence — the graha is not enumerated in this witness
entries.note: Atharvavedapariśiṣṭa 26.5.6cd (avp-s1). NO BINOMIAL: the Cologne Monier-Williams headword madhūka was among the ten blocked by HTTP 429/403 and was not obtained from any other route, so this ledger carries no botanical identification for it. Where the mainstream sequence has khadira at position 3 (yajn-s1, mats-s1, agni-s1, garu-s1), this witness has madhuka — the first point at which the two sequences part. Boddupalli & Sastri note a 'Māndhuka' samidha at Taittirīya Saṃhitā 3-4-8.3 (bod-s2) in a chapter with no planetary assignment (bod-s3); whether that word is this word is not stated by any source in this ledger. A madhūka also stands in the Śāṅkhāyana Āgrahāyaṇī handful (sgs-s1), again non-planetary (sgs-s2).

entries.forWhat: position 4 in the Atharvavedapariśiṣṭa 26.5.6–5.7 sequence — the graha is not enumerated in this witness
entries.note: Atharvavedapariśiṣṭa 26.5.6cd (avp-s1). NO BINOMIAL: the Cologne headword nyagrodha was blocked by HTTP 429/403 and obtained from no other route. Boddupalli & Sastri name naiyagrōdha as the head of a four-wood group — naiyagrōdha, audumbara, aśvattha, plāka — at Taittirīya Saṃhitā 3-4-8.4 (bod-s1), in a chapter carrying no planetary assignment (bod-s3), but they supply no binomial for it in any snippet held here. Nyagrodha does not appear anywhere in the mainstream navagraha sequence.

entries.forWhat: position 5 in the Atharvavedapariśiṣṭa 26.5.6–5.7 sequence — the graha is not enumerated in this witness
entries.botanical: Ficus glomerata (MW 1899, mw-udumbara) / Ficus racemosa (Boddupalli & Sastri 2015, bod-s5, s.v. audumbara). Both carried; no source here equates them.
entries.note: Atharvavedapariśiṣṭa 26.5.6cd (avp-s1). Udumbara occurs in both sequences but at different positions — 5 here, 6 in the mainstream witnesses (yajn-s1, mats-s1, agni-s1, garu-s1). That is a comparison of two cited lists, not an assignment: the graha at position 5 of this witness is not named (avp-s2).

entries.note: Atharvavedapariśiṣṭa 26.5.7 (avp-s2). NO BINOMIAL: the Cologne headword plakṣa was blocked by HTTP 429/403 and obtained from no other route. Boddupalli & Sastri include 'plāka' — which the ledger's own note reads as plakṣa with diacritics lost in PDF extraction — in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā 3-4-8.4 four-wood group (bod-s1), a chapter with no planetary assignment (bod-s3). Plakṣa does not appear anywhere in the mainstream navagraha sequence.

entries.forWhat: position 7 in the Atharvavedapariśiṣṭa 26.5.6–5.7 sequence — the graha is not enumerated in this witness
entries.botanical: Ficus religiosa (Monier-Williams 1899, s.v. aśvattha, via the wisdomlib mirror; also Boddupalli & Sastri 2015)
entries.note: Atharvavedapariśiṣṭa 26.5.7 (avp-s2). NOTE WHAT THIS DOES AND DOES NOT SHOW: aśvattha, the word modern printings of the navagraha list give for Jupiter, does occur in a navagraha samidh verse — but in THIS witness, at position 7, with no graha named (avp-s2). The mainstream witnesses read pippala at position 5 and never read aśvattha at all (yajn-s1, mats-s1, agni-s1, agni-s3, garu-s1). MW gives aśvattha as the holy fig tree, Ficus religiosa, citing the Atharvaveda and Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, and adds that the upper araṇi is made of its wood (mw-asvattha); Boddupalli & Sastri give the same binomial (bod-s5) and include aśvattha in the Taittirīya four-wood group (bod-s1). Aśvattha also stands in the Bṛhatsaṃhitā 43.12 nīrājana five (bs-s1), which is not graha-assigned.

entries.forWhat: position 8 in the Atharvavedapariśiṣṭa 26.5.6–5.7 sequence — the graha is not enumerated in this witness
entries.sanskrit: gomaya (in the e-text's plural, gomayāni) — NOT A PLANT
entries.note: Atharvavedapariśiṣṭa 26.5.7 (avp-s2). TWO CAUTIONS ON THIS ROW. (1) The GRETIL e-text prints the string 'gomayānikuśāś ca' without word division; read as gomayāni + kuśāḥ it yields exactly nine items for nine grahas, which is why it is so read here — but that division is the compiler's reading of an undivided string, not the edition's, and no source in this ledger divides it. (2) On that reading the item is cow-dung, not a tree or a grass, so this witness's 'nine samidhs' are not nine woods. This ledger carries no lexicon entry for gomaya and no botanical or material identification for it beyond the word itself.

entries.forWhat: position 9 in the Atharvavedapariśiṣṭa 26.5.6–5.7 sequence — the graha is not enumerated in this witness
entries.english: 'the sacred grass used at certain religious ceremonies'; MW adds 'the Brāhmaṇas commonly call it darbha' (mw-kusa)
entries.note: Atharvavedapariśiṣṭa 26.5.7 (avp-s2), on the same word-division reading flagged at position 8. Kuśa closes both sequences: it is also last in the mainstream witnesses (yajn-s1, mats-s1, agni-s1, agni-s3, garu-s1). That the two divergent lists share their first two items and their last one is an observation about two cited texts, made here by the compiler; no scholar in this ledger has published the comparison.

gaps.whatWasFound: The only samidh list in the work is at BS 43.12, inside chapter 43 nīrājanādhyāyaḥ — the army-lustration rite — and it names FIVE woods (khadira, palāśa, udumbara, kāśmarya, aśvattha) with no graha assignment (bs-s1). The heading list contains a grahabhaktiyogādhyāya (ch. 16) but no graha-homa or graha-śānti chapter (bs-s2). The passage that looks most like a per-tree effect table sits in chapter 84, dantakāṣṭhalakṣaṇādhyāyaḥ, and is about TOOTH-STICKS, not homa fuel (bs-s3).

contestedPoints: TWO TIER A SEQUENCES, NOT ONE. Four witnesses give arka–palāśa–khadira–apāmārga–pippala–udumbara–śamī–dūrvā–kuśa (yajn-s1, mats-s1, agni-s1, agni-s3, garu-s1). The Atharvavedapariśiṣṭa 26.5.6–5.7 gives arka–palāśa–madhuka–nyagrodha–udumbara–plakṣa–aśvattha–gomaya(?)–kuśa (avp-s1, avp-s2). Both are Tier A, both are for the grahas, and both ship. Which is older, or whether either depends on the other, is not stated by any source in this ledger and is not asserted here.

THE DIVERGENCE IS THE COMPILER'S OWN READING. No published scholarship in this ledger compares the two sequences. Geslani 2018, the standard monograph on grahaśānti, was searched for and not obtained (bookseller and review pages only). The side-by-side reading above is exactly that — a reading of two primary e-texts — and it must not be cited onward as a scholarly finding.

JUPITER'S WOOD IS PIPPALA, NOT AŚVATTHA, IN EVERY TIER A WITNESS HERE (yajn-s1, mats-s1, agni-s1, agni-s3, garu-s1). The sequence as commonly printed today substitutes aśvattha. Aśvattha DOES occur in a navagraha samidh verse — but in the divergent Atharvavedapariśiṣṭa list, at position 7, with no graha named (avp-s2). This ledger contains no source equating pippala with aśvattha, so the equation is not made and Jupiter's row ships without a binomial.

MANUSCRIPT VARIANT AT AGNIPURĀṆA 164.8. Mitra's own footnote records that mss ga, gha and ña read 'khadiras tv apāmārgo 'tha' against his printed 'khadiro hy apāmārgotha' (agni-s2), and the Garuḍapurāṇa e-text prints that same variant reading (garu-s1). The variant does not move any plant to a different graha. Noting that the two e-texts agree here is the compiler's observation, not a published collation.

KHADIRA HAS THREE BINOMIALS ACROSS THREE TIERS: Mimosa catechu (MW 1899, mw-khadira), Acacia catechu (Boddupalli & Sastri 2015, Tier B, bod-s4), Senegalia catechu (IJCRT 2026, Tier C, ijcrt-s2). All three carry the epithet catechu; no source here states they are one taxon. All three are carried.

PALĀŚA: Butea frondosa (mw-palasa) against Butea monosperma (bod-s6). UDUMBARA: Ficus glomerata (mw-udumbara) against Ficus racemosa (bod-s5). In each case both are carried and neither is resolved, because no source in this ledger performs the synonymy.

ŚAMĪ IS CONTESTED INSIDE MONIER-WILLIAMS ITSELF: the entry gives Prosopis spicigera 'or (according to others) Mimosa suma' and does not choose (mw-sami). The dictionary's own hedge is preserved rather than tidied.

KUŚA: MW gives Poa cynosuroides Retz. and notes that the Brāhmaṇas call it darbha (mw-kusa); the 2026 navagraha-vāṭikā paper gives Ketu's plant as Imperata cylindrica, calling it 'Darbha or Thatch Grass' (ijcrt-s3, ijcrt-s4). Different taxon, different tier, and — decisively — a different practice: that paper's frame is a plant PLANTED in the north-west, not a stick burned, and it cites no Sanskrit locus for any assignment (ijcrt-s1, ijcrt-s5).

THE SAFETY DATUM AND THE BOTANICAL IDENTIFICATION ARE NOT ON THE SAME SPECIES. Monier-Williams identifies arka as Calotropis gigantea (mw-arka); the ocular-toxicity paper studied Calotropis procera (basak-s1). The ledger records that both are called arka/madār and does not merge them. No source here reports on smoke or combustion of either.

THE TIER C STRATUM LOSES ITEMS. The Kanchi Kamakoti paraphrase of the Matsya Purāṇa navagraha-yajña prints only EIGHT woods, and śamī is the missing one (kkm-s1) — though MatsP 93.27, the verse being paraphrased, has it (mats-s1). A Hindi ritual portal heads a section 'the nine plants of the navagraha' and then names only EIGHT grahas, omitting the Moon, while also listing Śani before Śukra (pp-s2); the same page's samagri section does carry all nine woods in the mainstream order (pp-s1).

THE TIER C STRATUM ALSO ADDS ITEMS — TO A DIFFERENT LIST. A second Kanchi Kamakoti compilation lists Arka, Palāśa, Apāmārga, Peepul, Gular, Śamī, Dūrvā, Bel and Vata as samidhs (kst-s1). Bel and Vata are in no Tier A navagraha verse here, khadira is absent, and the ledger's own note records that this is a GENERAL homa list, not graha-assigned. It is recorded as a conflation hazard, not as a variant of the navagraha nine.

ONE TIER C SOURCE DOCUMENTS ITS OWN UNRELIABILITY. A ritual-guide page instructs its writers to quote Bṛhat Parāśara Horā Śāstra 23.1-17 or the Navagraha Kalpa-druma 'to include authority and SEO value' (shl-s1), and elsewhere asserts nine specific samidhs without naming one of them (shl-s2). That is direct evidence about how citations are generated on this stratum, and it is the reason no row in this dossier rests on a Tier C source alone.

THE NINE ARE NOT ALL WOODS. Positions 8 and 9 of the mainstream sequence are grasses — MW glosses dūrvā as bent/panic grass (mw-durva) and kuśa as a ceremonial grass (mw-kusa) — and Dutt's 1908 translation calls them 'blades' rather than twigs (gdutt-s1). In the Atharvavedapariśiṣṭa sequence position 8, on the word-division reading adopted here, is cow-dung. 'The nine sacred woods' is a convenient English label, not what the texts say.

'GOMAYĀNIKUŚĀŚ' IS UNDIVIDED IN THE E-TEXT. Reading it as gomayāni + kuśāḥ yields exactly nine items for nine grahas (avp-s2); that division is the compiler's and no source in this ledger performs it. If the division is wrong, the Atharvavedapariśiṣṭa list has eight items and the whole alignment shifts.

THE FOUR FIG-FAMILY WOODS AT AV-PARIŚIṢṬA POSITIONS 4–7 (nyagrodha, udumbara, plakṣa, aśvattha) are the same four Boddupalli & Sastri call the 'naiyagrōdha samidhas' of Taittirīya Saṃhitā 3-4-8.4 (bod-s1), a chapter they state carries no planetary assignment (bod-s3). THIS IS A COMPILER'S OBSERVATION ABOUT TWO CITED LISTS AND NOTHING MORE — no scholar in this ledger draws the connection, and no direction of borrowing is claimed or implied.

THE NINE-SAMIDHA SET IS A LIVE RETAIL CATEGORY AND A LIVE RITE. A commercial homam set advertises that each type of wood is associated with a particular graha (giri-s1); another vendor sells the nine as a single packet; a Hindi portal states that different plants' wood and leaves are used for each graha's śānti pūjā (pp-s3). This is a practice carried on now, not a closed historical record — but none of these sources names a text.
